extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters (city reporters, obituary writers, and weather beat reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom guidance on composing coherent, readable obituaries and on gathering, structuring, and writing timely weather stories for newspapers. Covers structure, sourcing, angles, common pitfalls, and stylistic cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must highlight the subject's most interesting aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should suggest why the person was interesting beyond a mundane job description; otherwise readers may not read the piece at length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leads that only state an ordinary occupation (e.g., 'druggist') if there is a more interesting facet (former lodge master, inventor, etc.). The lead should entice readers to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize a single theme or impression
rubrics_metrics.description: An obituary should emphasize throughout a single theme or impression to 'give the reader something to remember the man by.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a unifying idea (e.g., 'a man of perpetual activity') that illuminates disparate facts and ties career aspects together so the story feels coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a rigid block structure for obituaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the obituary in blocks rather than scattering elements: (i) lead (with news identification and circumstances of death), (2) genealogy/relatives list, (3) funeral arrangements, (4) biographical sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep each element together (e.g., genealogy in contiguous paragraphs) to avoid forcing readers to reassemble scattered facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select an overall block arrangement to fit subject and readership
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several valid block sequences (four designs) — choose based on how well known the subject is and biography length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1) lead → genealogy → funeral → biography for indisputably high-interest persons; 2) lead → biography → funeral → relatives when biography must establish importance; 3) lead → highlights → relatives → funeral → details for long biographies where many readers only want highlights; 4) lead → condensed biography → detailed biography → relatives → genealogy when keeping two-part biography close is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical sketch order: chronological or reverse chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: The biography can proceed chronologically from birth to death or in reverse chronology (death/recent career back to birth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse chronology is preferable for people important but not prominent or whose main work was recent — it links the subject to 'today' and attracts casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple careers, divide biography into separate blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject had several careers, present each career as its own block so each field is complete and does not spill into others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify diverse activities into divisions and present each fully and separately (e.g., business, churchwork, chess), avoiding overlap that injures coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dispersive, disorganized information
rubrics_metrics.description: Coherence is essential; obituaries that 'shovel' a mass of facts dispersively and demand readers fit them into order are failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material logically around the chosen theme and block structure so readers can follow without reassembling fragmented details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish sentence structure; vary sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor obits often have monotonous sentence patterns (repeated 'he' subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence beginnings and constructions to avoid a tiresome, repetitive rhythm and to maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superlatives and limit comparatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Superlatives are almost always inaccurate; comparatives should be used sparingly and only for 'double-strength' facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may contradict grand claims (e.g., 'the most successful furniture dealer'), so reserve strong adjectives for demonstrable, exceptional facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat weather stories as front-page, high-priority copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather stories are often top-column/page-1 copy because weather affects everyone and can displace other news in prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the public importance of weather copy and prepare to give it priority in scheduling and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the city: use revealing local places as weather indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter must know which streets/locations best reveal the effects of a storm (e.g., hills that ice over, sewers that clog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain lists of places to check for different weather types; local knowledge saves time and yields telling eyewitness material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Police station — check for accidents and traffic mishaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Police provide information on accidents and traffic-related consequences of snow, sleet, rain, heat, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect more automobile mishaps in precipitation/storms and tailor police queries to likely weather effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Fire station — inquire about fires related to weather (chimney, furnace problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire houses can yield winter news (chimney fires from uncleaned furnaces) and other weather-related incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about incidents that spike in specific weather (cold snaps, extreme use of heating) and related rescues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Hospitals — collect weather-linked injuries and illnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospitals report freezings, frostbite, slips and falls, heart failures from shoveling, sunstrokes, drownings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hospital data to quantify human costs and give vivid case examples for stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: City street department — ask about clearing, sanding, costs, street prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Street departments can say how many trucks/plows/shovelers were used, which streets were tackled first, and the cost of operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get specific metrics (tons of sand/cinders, number of plows) and reasons for street-priority decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: City sewer department — probe flood and drainage problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Sewer departments are vital for cloud-burst/high-water stories: which streets flooded, duration, and drainage measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sewer reports to document street-level flooding and impacts on neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: City park department — ask about parks, skating rinks, pools, and seasonal facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Park departments provide summertime attendance/activities and winter conditions for skating, toboggan slides, ski jumps, municipal courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include park usage details and how weather affected public recreation assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Transit (street railway/railroads/bus/airports) — check schedule maintenance and trouble locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transit operators report where and why schedules failed and how or when service will be restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get specifics on affected lines, times, and remedial actions to inform commuters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: County and state highway departments — check outside-city road conditions and tie-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Highway departments report on rural road blockages, washouts, and expected clearance times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use their info to portray regional extent and economic/transport effects beyond city limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Utilities and communications (electric, telephone, telegraph) — check outages and repair status
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities can say where lines are down, when repairs will finish, manpower involved, and estimated costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also ask radio stations which network programs were lost and what alternate circuits were used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Hotels — learn how many stranded people had to stay overnight
rubrics_metrics.description: Hotels report on commuters or visitors unable to get home because of weather and related demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hotel reports to humanize stories — stranded theatergoers, commuters, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Garages — check business effects and demand for warm storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Garages can report frantic motorists, rates paid for storage, and incidents related to extreme cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use garage anecdotes to illustrate public reaction and commercial impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Stores — check business volume changes and demand for weather goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Stores can report declines in some business and spikes in sales of galoshes, umbrellas, swim suits, or fuel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify sales increases or shortages to show economic effects on retailers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: Weather Bureau — consult for causes and official outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: The Weather Bureau explains why the weather occurred and provides official forecasts and expectations of return to normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bureau analysis for authoritative cause-and-effect and to ground forecasts in official data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: County agricultural agent — check crop damage and future prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: Agricultural agents report storm impacts on current crops and prospects for the next season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include agricultural consequences for rural readers and local economies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to inspect the scene or rely on telephone reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to go on location depends on how well the reporter knows the city and how much a personal inspection will add beyond telephone information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If telephone detail suggests a dramatic on-site scene (e.g., a bus blocked a mile long), inspect; if vague (e.g., 'Box 723 — chimney fire') refrain from unnecessary exposure to hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with the county editor and photographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with the county editor to combine nearby towns' reports into a 'with story' and coordinate with photographers so story and pictures overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call police/dispatch to direct photographers to locations while the scene remains photogenic; combine correspondent dispatches for broader coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every-story essentials for weather copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Each weather story must answer: (1) When did it start? (2) Just how bad is it? (3) What caused it? (4) How long will it last?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers want precise timing, severity, causes, and duration — get timestamps, measurements, and official forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'freaks of geography' judiciously and label them
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring local peculiarities (ponds, hills, microclimates) are useful but should be explicitly labeled as freaks and not presented as representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect these familiar reference points; don't overuse selective thermometers to make conditions seem worse — that's faking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peg the weather story on one of six effective angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hang the story on one angle: (1) results of the weather, (2) causes, (3) the forecast, (4) the extent, (5) comparison/contrast with the past, (6) curious/unusual aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the angle that best serves reader interest: results and extent for spectacle; forecast for practical need; comparisons if recent memories exist; curios for color but not as the backbone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common pitfalls in weather writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitfalls include bromidic/clichéd wording (e.g., 'Jack Frost' clichés), regional mismatches (using coastal epigrams inland), issuing unofficial forecasts, and over-long-ago comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor language to the region, avoid stale metaphors, label any personal forecast as such (federal law restricts issuing forecasts that could be mistaken for official ones), and compare with recent weather readers recall rather than events too old to be meaningful.
